note: Written and checked by hand. Each question: four options with the right answer first, a hint and an explanation shown after answering. today-pick.mjs chooses five a day and shuffles the options. Titles of works are marked *thus* and set in italics.

questions.question: Which play contains the stage direction “Exit, pursued by a bear”?
questions.hint: A statue appears to come to life in its last scene.
questions.explanation: Antigonus leaves the baby Perdita on the coast of Bohemia in Act 3, scene 3 of *The Winter’s Tale* and is chased off by a bear. A shepherd’s son later reports that the bear has eaten him.

questions.question: Which two people watch Lady Macbeth sleepwalking in Act 5, scene 1 of *Macbeth*?
questions.hint: One of them says the disease is “beyond my practice”.
questions.explanation: A waiting-gentlewoman has called in a doctor of physic. They see Lady Macbeth rub her hands and hear her speak of Duncan’s blood and Lady Macduff’s death.

questions.question: Which play does Hamlet ask the travelling players to perform before Claudius?
questions.hint: Hamlet tells the King its other title is “The Mousetrap”.
questions.explanation: Hamlet asks the players for *The Murder of Gonzago* and adds “some dozen or sixteen lines” of his own. The play shows a king poisoned in his garden, as the Ghost says Old Hamlet was.

questions.question: Whose skull does Hamlet hold in the graveyard scene?
questions.hint: He was the king’s jester.
questions.explanation: The First Gravedigger says the skull has lain in the earth twenty-three years and belonged to Yorick, the King’s jester. Hamlet remembers being carried on his back.

questions.question: In which play do Rosalind, Orlando and Touchstone appear?
questions.hint: Much of it takes place in the Forest of Arden.
questions.explanation: Rosalind is banished from her uncle’s court and goes to the Forest of Arden disguised as a young man, Ganymede, with her cousin Celia and the court fool Touchstone.

questions.question: In *Othello*, what is the handkerchief Othello gave Desdemona embroidered with?
questions.hint: Iago describes it to Othello in Act 3, scene 3.
questions.explanation: Iago calls it a handkerchief “spotted with strawberries”. Emilia picks it up when Desdemona drops it and gives it to Iago, who leaves it in Cassio’s lodging.

questions.question: In *The Tempest*, who imprisoned Ariel in a cloven pine before Prospero came to the island?
questions.hint: She was Caliban’s mother.
questions.explanation: Prospero reminds Ariel that the witch Sycorax confined him in a pine for twelve years, and that he released him. Sycorax had died before Prospero arrived.

questions.question: In *Twelfth Night*, what colour stockings does the forged letter tell Malvolio to wear?
questions.hint: He is also told to wear them cross-gartered.
questions.explanation: Maria writes the letter in a hand like Olivia’s. It tells Malvolio to wear yellow stockings, cross-gartered, and to smile, all things Olivia dislikes.

questions.question: Who says “A plague o’ both your houses!” in *Romeo and Juliet*?
questions.hint: He is fatally wounded when Romeo steps between him and his opponent.
questions.explanation: Mercutio is stabbed by Tybalt under Romeo’s arm in Act 3, scene 1. He curses both the Montagues and the Capulets before he dies.

questions.question: Who begins a speech “Friends, Romans, countrymen, lend me your ears”?
questions.hint: He has been given permission to speak at Caesar’s funeral.
questions.explanation: Mark Antony speaks after Brutus in Act 3, scene 2 of *Julius Caesar*. By repeating that Brutus is “an honourable man” he turns the crowd against the conspirators.

questions.question: In *Much Ado About Nothing*, who is the constable of the Watch?
questions.hint: He is famous for using the wrong word.
questions.explanation: Dogberry and his partner Verges lead the Watch, who overhear Borachio boasting about the plot against Hero. Dogberry’s muddled language delays the truth coming out.

questions.question: In *The Merchant of Venice*, which casket holds Portia’s portrait?
questions.hint: Its inscription says “Who chooseth me must give and hazard all he hath.”
questions.explanation: Morocco chooses gold and Arragon silver. Bassanio chooses lead and finds Portia’s picture inside.

questions.question: In *A Midsummer Night’s Dream*, what does Puck give Bottom in place of his own head?
questions.hint: Quince cries out that Bottom is “translated”.
questions.explanation: Puck transforms Bottom while the workmen rehearse their play in the wood. Titania, under the spell of the love-juice, wakes and falls in love with him.

link.label: A Midsummer Night’s Dream study guide

questions.question: Which play opens “Now is the winter of our discontent / Made glorious summer by this sun of York”?
questions.hint: The speaker is the Duke of Gloucester.
questions.explanation: Richard, Duke of Gloucester, speaks the opening soliloquy alone on stage. The “sun of York” is his brother, King Edward IV.

questions.question: Before which battle does Henry V speak about St Crispin’s Day?
questions.hint: It was fought on 25 October 1415.
questions.explanation: Henry speaks in Act 4, scene 3, when Westmorland wishes they had more men. The battle of Agincourt was fought on the feast of Saints Crispin and Crispinian.

questions.question: In which year was the First Folio of Shakespeare’s plays published?
questions.hint: It came out seven years after his death.
questions.explanation: *Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies* was published in 1623. It contains thirty-six plays, eighteen of which had not been printed before, *Macbeth* and *The Tempest* among them.

questions.question: Which two actors gathered the plays for the First Folio?
questions.hint: Both were fellow members of Shakespeare’s company and are named in his will.
questions.explanation: Heminges and Condell, of the King’s Men, signed the dedication and the address “To the great Variety of Readers”. Shakespeare left each of them money to buy a memorial ring.

questions.question: To whom is the 1609 edition of Shakespeare’s Sonnets dedicated?
questions.hint: The dedication was signed by the publisher, Thomas Thorpe.
questions.explanation: The dedication names “the onlie begetter of these insuing sonnets Mr. W. H.”. Who W. H. was has never been settled.

questions.question: Which is usually described as Shakespeare’s shortest play?
questions.hint: It has two pairs of identical twins.
questions.explanation: *The Comedy of Errors* has fewer than 1,800 lines. *Macbeth* is the shortest of the tragedies.

questions.question: During a performance of which play did the first Globe Theatre burn down in 1613?
questions.hint: A cannon was fired to mark a king’s entrance.
questions.explanation: On 29 June 1613 a stage cannon set light to the thatch during *Henry VIII*, then known as *All Is True*. Contemporary letters report that nobody was killed.

questions.question: What did Shakespeare leave his wife, Anne, in his will?
questions.hint: The bequest was added between the lines of the will.
questions.explanation: The will of 1616 leaves Anne “my second best bed with the furniture”. Most of the estate went to his elder daughter, Susanna.

questions.question: What is the name of Coriolanus’s mother?
questions.hint: She persuades him not to attack Rome.
questions.explanation: Volumnia, with Coriolanus’s wife Virgilia and his son, pleads with him outside Rome in Act 5, scene 3. He gives way, knowing it will cost him his life.

questions.question: At the start of *Titus Andronicus*, Tamora is queen of which people?
questions.hint: Titus has brought her to Rome as a prisoner of war.
questions.explanation: Titus returns from war against the Goths with Tamora and her sons as captives. He has her eldest son, Alarbus, sacrificed, which begins her revenge.

questions.question: In which city is *Measure for Measure* set?
questions.hint: Its duke leaves Angelo in charge and stays in disguise.
questions.explanation: Duke Vincentio hands power to Angelo and remains in Vienna dressed as a friar. Angelo revives a law against fornication and condemns Claudio to death.

questions.question: Who is the drunken tinker tricked into believing he is a lord in the Induction to *The Taming of the Shrew*?
questions.hint: He is found asleep outside an alehouse.
questions.explanation: A lord finds Christopher Sly asleep and has him dressed and served as a nobleman. The story of Katherina and Petruchio is then performed for him as a play.

link.label: The Taming of the Shrew study guide

questions.question: In *Love’s Labour’s Lost*, for how long do the King of Navarre and his lords swear to study and keep away from women?
questions.hint: Berowne says the oath is impossible to keep almost as soon as he signs it.
questions.explanation: The King, Berowne, Longaville and Dumaine swear a three-year oath. The Princess of France and her ladies arrive on an embassy at once.

questions.question: Which writer is generally thought to have written the first two acts of *Pericles*?
questions.hint: He also published a prose version of the story in 1608.
questions.explanation: Most editors accept that *Pericles* was written with George Wilkins. Wilkins’s prose *The Painful Adventures of Pericles* appeared in 1608.

questions.question: Which king did the historical Macbeth defeat and kill in 1040?
questions.hint: Shakespeare makes him an old man killed in his bed.
questions.explanation: The historical Duncan was a young king killed in battle near Elgin. Macbeth then ruled Alba until 1057, when he was killed by Duncan’s son Malcolm.

questions.question: Which early printed text of *Hamlet* is much the shortest?
questions.hint: In it, Polonius is called Corambis.
questions.explanation: The First Quarto is a little over half the length of the Second Quarto. Some scholars think it is a reconstruction from memory, others an early version.

questions.question: Elsinore, where *Hamlet* is set, is the English name for which Danish town?
questions.hint: Its castle, Kronborg, guards the sound between Denmark and Sweden.
questions.explanation: Kronborg Castle at Helsingør was rebuilt in the 1570s and 1580s. English actors, Will Kemp among them, performed at the Danish court there in the 1580s.

questions.question: Who wrote notes on a performance of *Macbeth* at the Globe in April 1611?
questions.hint: He was an astrologer and doctor.
questions.explanation: Simon Forman’s “Booke of Plaies” describes Macbeth and Banquo meeting three women in a wood and Lady Macbeth trying to wash her hands. It is the earliest account of the play in performance.

questions.question: Which Swiss traveller saw *Julius Caesar* on Bankside in September 1599?
questions.hint: He was a medical student from Basel.
questions.explanation: Thomas Platter wrote that he saw “the tragedy of the first Emperor Julius Caesar” in a thatched playhouse across the river on 21 September 1599. It is probably the new Globe.

questions.question: Which play did Samuel Pepys call “the most insipid ridiculous play that ever I saw in my life”?
questions.hint: He did admit to liking the dancing and some “handsome women”.
questions.explanation: Pepys saw *A Midsummer Night’s Dream* at the King’s Theatre on 29 September 1662 and recorded his verdict in his diary that night.

link.label: A Midsummer Night’s Dream study guide

questions.question: In Nahum Tate’s 1681 version of *King Lear*, whom does Cordelia marry?
questions.hint: Tate removed the Fool and gave the play a happy ending.
questions.explanation: In Tate’s *History of King Lear*, Lear is restored to his throne and Cordelia marries Edgar. Tate’s version held the stage until the nineteenth century.

questions.question: Which English poem of 1562 was Shakespeare’s main source for *Romeo and Juliet*?
options: *The Tragicall Historye of Romeus and Juliet*
questions.hint: Its author, Arthur Brooke, drowned in the following year.
questions.explanation: Arthur Brooke’s long poem tells the story over about nine months. Shakespeare compresses the action into a few days.

questions.question: Shakespeare took the story of *Othello* from a tale by which Italian writer?
questions.hint: The tale appears in his collection *Gli Hecatommithi* of 1565.
questions.explanation: In Cinthio’s tale only Disdemona is named. The other characters are known by their roles, the Moor and the Ensign.

questions.question: For his Roman plays Shakespeare read Plutarch in whose English translation?
questions.hint: It was translated from Jacques Amyot’s French.
questions.explanation: North’s *Lives of the Noble Grecians and Romanes* was published in 1579. Some speeches in *Antony and Cleopatra* and *Coriolanus* follow North’s wording closely.

questions.question: The Porter in *Macbeth* jokes about an “equivocator”. Which Jesuit, executed in 1606, is usually thought to lie behind the joke?
questions.hint: He was tried after the Gunpowder Plot.
questions.explanation: Henry Garnet defended equivocation, the practice of giving misleading answers under oath, in his trial in March 1606. He was executed in May.

questions.question: When Hamlet speaks of making his “quietus” with “a bare bodkin”, what is a bodkin?
questions.hint: He is thinking about suicide.
questions.explanation: In the “To be, or not to be” soliloquy a bodkin is a short dagger. A quietus is the settling of an account.

questions.question: In *Macbeth*, what is a thane?
options: A Scottish nobleman holding land from the king
A priest of the old religion
questions.hint: Macbeth is already Thane of Glamis when the play begins.
questions.explanation: A thane held land directly from the king. The witches hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor and king.

questions.question: In *Hamlet*, who are the “groundlings”?
options: Spectators who stood in the yard of the playhouse
questions.hint: They paid the lowest price for admission.
questions.explanation: Hamlet complains of actors who “split the ears of the groundlings”, the audience standing around the stage for a penny.

questions.question: Which of King Lear’s daughters refuses to compete in praising him?
questions.hint: Her answer is “Nothing, my lord.”
questions.explanation: Cordelia says she loves Lear “according to my bond, no more nor less”. He divides her share of the kingdom between her sisters.

questions.question: How does Cleopatra die?
options: By the bite of an asp
questions.hint: A clown brings her a basket of figs.
questions.explanation: Cleopatra puts asps to her breast and arm in Act 5, scene 2. Plutarch reports that the cause of her death was uncertain, though the asp was the common story.

questions.question: Whose anger does the first line of the *Iliad* announce as its subject?
questions.hint: He withdraws from the fighting after a quarrel over a captive woman.
questions.explanation: The poem opens with the anger of Achilles, son of Peleus, against Agamemnon, who has taken Briseis from him. Samuel Butler translates the first words as “Sing, O goddess, the anger of Achilles”.

questions.question: What is the name of Odysseus’s old dog, who recognises him on his return to Ithaca?
questions.hint: He is lying neglected on a dung heap.
questions.explanation: Argos wags his tail and drops his ears when he sees Odysseus, disguised as a beggar, and then dies. Odysseus hides a tear from Eumaeus.

questions.question: What name does Odysseus give the Cyclops Polyphemus?
questions.hint: It means the other Cyclopes think Polyphemus is not being attacked at all.
questions.explanation: In Greek the name is Outis. When Polyphemus shouts that Nobody is killing him, the other Cyclopes go away. Butler’s translation renders the name as “Noman”.

questions.question: Penelope tells her suitors she will choose a husband when she has finished weaving a shroud. Whose shroud is it?
questions.hint: He is still alive, living on his farm.
questions.explanation: Penelope weaves by day and unpicks the work by night for three years, until one of her maids tells the suitors.

questions.question: Odysseus angers which god by blinding the Cyclops Polyphemus?
questions.hint: Polyphemus is his son.
questions.explanation: Polyphemus prays to his father Poseidon, who keeps Odysseus from home for years. Athena supports Odysseus throughout.

questions.question: The *Iliad* ends with the funeral of which hero?
questions.hint: His father, Priam, comes to Achilles’ tent at night to ransom the body.
questions.explanation: The last line of the poem is “Thus, then, did they celebrate the funeral of Hector tamer of horses” in Butler’s translation. The death of Achilles is not narrated.

questions.question: In Book 6 of the *Iliad*, why does Hector’s baby son Astyanax cry when his father reaches for him?
options: He is frightened by the plume on Hector’s helmet
questions.hint: Hector laughs and takes the helmet off.
questions.explanation: Hector has come in from the fighting to see Andromache. He lays down the helmet, kisses the boy and prays that he will be a better man than his father.

questions.question: Whom does Aeneas carry on his shoulders out of burning Troy?
questions.hint: He leads his son by the hand at the same time.
questions.explanation: Aeneas carries Anchises, who holds the household gods, and leads Ascanius. His wife Creusa is lost in the confusion and appears to him later as a ghost.

questions.question: According to the ancient lives of Virgil, he asked for the unfinished *Aeneid* to be burned. Who overruled him?
questions.hint: The poem tells of the founding of the Roman people.
questions.explanation: Virgil died in 19 BC with the poem unrevised. The emperor ordered his literary executors, Varius and Tucca, to publish it.

questions.question: Which queen falls in love with Aeneas and kills herself when he leaves?
questions.hint: Her city is in North Africa.
questions.explanation: Mercury reminds Aeneas that he is meant to found a new home in Italy, and he sails from Carthage. Dido dies on a pyre in Book 4.

questions.question: In *The Authoress of the Odyssey* (1897), Samuel Butler argued that the poem was written by whom?
questions.hint: He thought she put herself into the poem as Nausicaa.
questions.explanation: Butler placed the author at Trapani in western Sicily. He went on to translate the *Iliad* (1898) and the *Odyssey* (1900) into prose.

questions.question: In how many books was *Paradise Lost* first published in 1667?
questions.hint: The second edition, of 1674, divided two of them.
questions.explanation: Milton split Books 7 and 10 for the 1674 edition, making twelve books, the number in Virgil’s *Aeneid*.

questions.question: Who says “Better to reign in Hell, than serve in Heav’n” in *Paradise Lost*?
questions.hint: He has just woken in the burning lake.
questions.explanation: Satan says it in Book 1, after he and Beelzebub have raised themselves from the burning lake.

questions.question: For how many years does Faustus’s pact give him the service of Mephistopheles?
questions.hint: Faustus signs the deed in his own blood.
questions.explanation: At the end of the twenty-four years Faustus waits for his last hour to strike and the devils come for him.

questions.question: In *Doctor Faustus*, whose face “launched a thousand ships”?
questions.hint: Mephistopheles makes a spirit appear in her shape.
questions.explanation: Faustus says “Was this the face that launched a thousand ships / And burnt the topless towers of Ilium?” when the spirit of Helen appears, near the end of the play.

questions.question: Christopher Marlowe was killed in 1593 in which place?
questions.hint: He had spent the day at a house there with three other men.
questions.explanation: Marlowe was stabbed by Ingram Frizer at the house of Eleanor Bull in Deptford on 30 May 1593. The coroner’s inquest found that Frizer acted in self-defence.

questions.question: In *The Duchess of Malfi*, who says “Cover her face; mine eyes dazzle: she died young”?
questions.hint: He ordered her death.
questions.explanation: Ferdinand speaks over the Duchess’s body in Act 4, scene 2. Soon afterwards he turns on Bosola, who carried out the murder.

questions.question: In which language did Thomas More first publish *Utopia* in 1516?
questions.hint: The first English translation appeared in 1551, after More’s execution.
questions.explanation: *Utopia* was printed at Louvain in 1516. Ralph Robinson’s English translation was published in 1551.

questions.question: Who describes the island of Utopia in More’s book?
questions.hint: He is a traveller said to have sailed with Amerigo Vespucci.
questions.explanation: More meets Raphael Hythloday in Antwerp through his friend Peter Giles. The surname combines Greek words usually translated as “expert in nonsense”.

questions.question: To whom did Machiavelli dedicate *The Prince*?
questions.hint: He was the grandson of Lorenzo the Magnificent.
questions.explanation: Machiavelli dedicated the book to Lorenzo di Piero de’ Medici, hoping to return to public service after the Medici came back to power in Florence in 1512.

questions.question: Machiavelli wrote *The Prince* in about 1513. When was it first printed?
questions.hint: Machiavelli had been dead for five years.
questions.explanation: *The Prince* circulated in manuscript and was printed in 1532. In 1559 it was placed on the Church’s Index of Prohibited Books.

questions.question: *Arden of Faversham* dramatises a real murder of 1551. Who arranged the killing of Thomas Arden?
options: His wife, Alice, and her lover
questions.hint: The case was told in Holinshed’s *Chronicles*.
questions.explanation: Alice Arden and her lover Mosby hired killers, among them Black Will and Shakebag. Alice was burned at Canterbury in 1551.

questions.question: In the manuscript of the play *Sir Thomas More*, which section is widely believed to be in Shakespeare’s handwriting?
questions.hint: In those pages More calms a riot against foreigners in London.
questions.explanation: Several writers revised the play. Three pages in the hand known as Hand D are widely accepted as Shakespeare’s, which would make them the only surviving literary manuscript in his hand.

questions.question: To whom did Shakespeare dedicate *Venus and Adonis* in 1593?
questions.hint: He dedicated *The Rape of Lucrece* to the same man a year later.
questions.explanation: Both poems are dedicated to Henry Wriothesley, third Earl of Southampton. *Venus and Adonis* was the first work published under Shakespeare’s name.

questions.question: The short, rapidly rhyming lines known as “Skeltonics” are named after which poet?
questions.hint: He was tutor to the young Henry VIII.
questions.explanation: John Skelton wrote in short lines that keep the same rhyme for as long as he can find words for it, as in *Phyllyp Sparowe* and *Colyn Cloute*.

questions.question: In *Gulliver’s Travels*, what are the Houyhnhnms?
questions.hint: Gulliver visits them in the fourth and last voyage.
questions.explanation: The Houyhnhnms rule a land where the Yahoos, animals in human shape, are their servants. Gulliver returns home unable to bear human company.

questions.question: Lilliput and Blefuscu go to war over which end to break what?
questions.hint: The two parties are the Big-Endians and the Little-Endians.
questions.explanation: Swift’s quarrel over eggs mocks religious and political disputes in England, including the division between Catholics and Protestants.

questions.question: When *Gulliver’s Travels* was published in 1726, whose name appeared as the author?
questions.hint: Swift wanted the book to look like a real traveller’s account.
questions.explanation: The title page reads “By Lemuel Gulliver, First a Surgeon, and then a Captain of several Ships”. Swift arranged publication anonymously through intermediaries.

questions.question: Why does Robinson Crusoe call the man he rescues Friday?
options: Because that is the day he saves him
Because it is the man’s own name
Because Friday is a holy day
Because he arrives on the sixth day of a storm
questions.hint: Crusoe keeps a calendar on a wooden post.
questions.explanation: Crusoe saves the man from a group of cannibals and names him after the day of the rescue. He teaches him English and the Christian religion.

questions.question: Which Scottish sailor, marooned on a Pacific island from 1704 to 1709, is often named as an inspiration for *Robinson Crusoe*?
questions.hint: He had asked to be put ashore after a quarrel with his captain.
questions.explanation: Selkirk lived alone on Más a Tierra in the Juan Fernández Islands until Woodes Rogers’s ships took him off. Rogers and Richard Steele both published accounts of him before Defoe’s novel of 1719.

questions.question: Where is most of Aphra Behn’s *Oroonoko* set?
questions.hint: It was an English colony until it was handed to the Dutch in 1667.
questions.explanation: Oroonoko, an African prince, is tricked into slavery and taken to Surinam. Behn’s narrator claims to have witnessed the events there.

questions.question: In *A Room of One’s Own*, on whose tomb does Woolf say “all women together ought to let flowers fall”?
questions.hint: Woolf notes that the tomb is in Westminster Abbey.
questions.explanation: Woolf writes that Aphra Behn “earned them the right to speak their minds”, as one of the first English women to earn her living by writing.

questions.question: *The Rape of the Lock* grew out of a quarrel after Lord Petre cut a lock of hair from which woman?
questions.hint: In the poem she becomes Belinda.
questions.explanation: John Caryll suggested Pope write a poem to make peace between the two Catholic families. The first version appeared in 1712 and the longer one, with the sylphs, in 1714.

link.label: The Rape of the Lock and An Essay on Criticism

questions.question: Which poem by Alexander Pope contains the line “A little learning is a dang’rous thing”?
questions.hint: Pope published it in 1711, when he was twenty-three.
questions.explanation: The poem continues “Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring”. The same poem contains “To err is human, to forgive divine.”

questions.question: What is the subtitle of Samuel Richardson’s *Pamela* (1740)?
questions.hint: Henry Fielding mocked it in *Shamela*.
questions.explanation: Pamela Andrews, a servant, resists her master Mr B. and eventually marries him. Fielding’s parody, *An Apology for the Life of Mrs. Shamela Andrews*, appeared in 1741.

questions.question: When was Thomas Paine’s pamphlet *Common Sense* published?
questions.hint: It came out six months before the Declaration of Independence.
questions.explanation: *Common Sense* was published in Philadelphia on 10 January 1776 and argued for independence from Britain. It sold in very large numbers in its first year.

link.label: Common Sense and The American Crisis

questions.question: Which work of Thomas Paine opens “These are the times that try men’s souls”?
questions.hint: It was written during the retreat across New Jersey in December 1776.
questions.explanation: Washington is said to have had the first *American Crisis* paper read to his troops before they crossed the Delaware on Christmas night 1776.

link.label: Common Sense and The American Crisis

questions.question: Which book, published days after Charles I’s execution in 1649, presented itself as the king’s own meditations?
questions.hint: Milton wrote a reply to it called *Eikonoklastes*.
questions.explanation: *Eikon Basilike* went through dozens of editions in 1649. How much of it Charles wrote himself has been argued over ever since.

questions.question: At which house near Geneva did Mary Shelley begin *Frankenstein* in the summer of 1816?
questions.hint: Lord Byron had rented it.
questions.explanation: Byron proposed that each of the party write a ghost story. Mary Shelley’s became *Frankenstein*, and John Polidori’s became *The Vampyre*.

questions.question: What is the subtitle of *Frankenstein*?
questions.hint: In Greek myth the original stole fire from the gods.
questions.explanation: *Frankenstein; or, The Modern Prometheus* was published anonymously on 1 January 1818. Mary Shelley revised it for the edition of 1831.

questions.question: At which university does Victor Frankenstein study natural philosophy?
questions.hint: It was in Bavaria.
questions.explanation: Victor leaves Geneva for Ingolstadt at seventeen. There he builds the creature in a lodging he calls his “workshop of filthy creation”.

questions.question: Which family does the creature watch through a gap in the wall of a cottage?
questions.hint: He learns to speak and read by listening to them.
questions.explanation: The creature hides in a hovel beside the De Laceys’ cottage for months. When he finally speaks to them, Felix drives him away.

questions.question: What was the original title of *Pride and Prejudice*?
questions.hint: Austen wrote the first version in 1796–97.
questions.explanation: Her father offered *First Impressions* to the publisher Thomas Cadell in 1797, who declined it unseen. It was revised and published as *Pride and Prejudice* in 1813.

questions.question: Which novel opens “It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife”?
questions.hint: The family it introduces has five daughters.
questions.explanation: The rest of the first chapter shows that it is Mrs Bennet, with five unmarried daughters, who is in want of a rich husband for one of them.

questions.question: How was the author of *Sense and Sensibility* identified on its title page in 1811?
questions.hint: It was the first of her novels to be published.
questions.explanation: None of Austen’s novels carried her name in her lifetime. *Pride and Prejudice* was published as “By the Author of *Sense and Sensibility*”.

questions.question: Which poem opened the first edition of *Lyrical Ballads* in 1798?
options: The Rime of the Ancyent Marinere
Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey
questions.hint: Wordsworth later moved it further back in the book.
questions.explanation: *Lyrical Ballads* was published anonymously by Wordsworth and Coleridge. Coleridge’s poem came first and Tintern Abbey last.

questions.question: What does the Ancient Mariner use to shoot the albatross?
questions.hint: “With my cross-bow / I shot the Albatross.”
questions.explanation: The Mariner kills the bird at the end of Part 1 without giving a reason. His shipmates hang it round his neck in Part 2.

link.label: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner study guide

questions.question: In which book of 1817 did Coleridge first print the prose notes in the margins of *The Rime of the Ancient Mariner*?
questions.hint: The title refers to the scattered prophecies of the Sibyl.
questions.explanation: The gloss is written in the voice of an old-fashioned editor commenting on the poem, and it sometimes says more than the verse does.

link.label: The Rime of the Ancient Mariner study guide

questions.question: Wordsworth’s Lines written a few miles above Tintern Abbey revisits the banks of which river?
questions.hint: It forms part of the border between England and Wales.
questions.explanation: Wordsworth dated the poem 13 July 1798 and recalled a first visit five years earlier. He walked there with his sister Dorothy, who is addressed at the end.

questions.question: Which of Blake’s poems asks “What immortal hand or eye / Could frame thy fearful symmetry?”
questions.hint: It belongs to *Songs of Experience*.
questions.explanation: Blake printed *Songs of Experience* with *Songs of Innocence* from 1794. The Tyger is often read beside The Lamb, its counterpart in Innocence.

link.label: Songs of Innocence and of Experience

questions.question: How did William Blake print *Songs of Innocence and of Experience*?
options: By relief etching on copper plates, coloured by hand
questions.hint: Text and pictures were made on the same plate.
questions.explanation: Blake wrote the text backwards on copper in an acid-resistant liquid and etched away the rest. He and his wife Catherine coloured each copy by hand, so no two are the same.

link.label: Songs of Innocence and of Experience

questions.question: What did young admirers of Goethe’s *Werther* copy from the novel’s hero?
options: His blue coat and yellow waistcoat
His habit of writing in French
questions.hint: Goethe describes the clothes in the novel.
questions.explanation: *The Sorrows of Young Werther* (1774) made Goethe famous across Europe. Werther dies wearing the blue coat and yellow waistcoat he wore when he first danced with Lotte.

questions.question: Under which name did Charlotte Brontë publish *Jane Eyre* in 1847?
questions.hint: Her sisters published as Ellis and Acton.
questions.explanation: The three sisters kept their initials. Emily published *Wuthering Heights* as Ellis Bell and Anne published *Agnes Grey* as Acton Bell in the same year.

questions.question: Who asks Jane Eyre to marry him and go with him to India as a missionary?
questions.hint: He turns out to be her cousin.
questions.explanation: Jane refuses to marry St John without love, though she offers to go to India as his assistant. She then hears Rochester’s voice calling her.

questions.question: Who tells most of the story of *Wuthering Heights* to Mr Lockwood?
questions.hint: She is the housekeeper at Thrushcross Grange.
questions.explanation: Lockwood, Heathcliff’s tenant, falls ill after a night at Wuthering Heights. Nelly Dean tells him the history of the two families while he recovers.

questions.question: In which magazine was *Great Expectations* first published?
questions.hint: Dickens owned and edited it himself.
questions.explanation: *Great Expectations* ran in weekly instalments from December 1860 to August 1861. Dickens had started the magazine in 1859.

questions.question: Who turns out to be Pip’s secret benefactor in *Great Expectations*?
questions.hint: Pip first meets him on the marshes on Christmas Eve.
questions.explanation: Abel Magwitch, the convict Pip helped as a child, made a fortune as a sheep-farmer in New South Wales and has paid for Pip’s education.

questions.question: Which novelist persuaded Dickens to change the ending of *Great Expectations*?
questions.hint: He was the author of *The Last Days of Pompeii*.
questions.explanation: In the first ending Pip and Estella meet briefly and part. Bulwer-Lytton thought it too sad, and Dickens wrote the version in which they leave the ruins of Satis House together.

questions.question: *A Christmas Carol* is divided into five staves. What is a stave?
questions.hint: The book is called a carol.
questions.explanation: Dickens used the word as another form of “stanza”, so the book is laid out like the verses of a carol. It was published on 19 December 1843.

questions.question: At whose Christmas party does the Ghost of Christmas Past show Scrooge his younger self?
questions.hint: He was Scrooge’s first employer.
questions.explanation: Scrooge had been apprenticed to Fezziwig. Watching the party makes him remember his own clerk, Bob Cratchit.

questions.question: At which English port does Dracula come ashore?
questions.hint: He leaps from a wrecked ship in the shape of a large dog.
questions.explanation: The Russian schooner Demeter runs aground with its dead captain lashed to the wheel. Stoker had stayed in Whitby in 1890 and found the name Dracula in a book in the town’s library.

questions.question: What is the name of the house near London that Dracula buys?
questions.hint: Jonathan Harker travels to Transylvania to complete the purchase.
questions.explanation: Carfax stands next to Dr Seward’s asylum at Purfleet. Dracula has boxes of earth sent there from his castle.

questions.question: Which lawyer’s inquiries frame *Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde*?
questions.hint: He holds Jekyll’s will.
questions.explanation: Utterson is disturbed that Jekyll’s will leaves everything to Edward Hyde. The full explanation comes only in the last two chapters, in Lanyon’s narrative and Jekyll’s statement.

questions.question: Which murder makes Hyde a wanted man?
options: The murder of Sir Danvers Carew
The murder of a child in the street
questions.hint: A maid witnesses it from a window by moonlight.
questions.explanation: Hyde beats Sir Danvers Carew, a Member of Parliament, to death with a heavy cane, half of which is found at the scene.

questions.question: In which magazine did *The Picture of Dorian Gray* first appear, in 1890?
questions.hint: It was based in Philadelphia.
questions.explanation: The magazine version has thirteen chapters. Wilde expanded it to twenty chapters, with a Preface, for the book of 1891.

link.label: The Picture of Dorian Gray study guide

questions.question: Who paints the portrait of Dorian Gray?
questions.hint: Dorian later kills him.
questions.explanation: Basil finishes the portrait in the first chapter. Years later Dorian shows him what the picture has become and stabs him.

link.label: The Picture of Dorian Gray study guide

questions.question: What is the subtitle of *Tess of the d’Urbervilles*?
questions.hint: Many reviewers objected to it.
questions.explanation: Hardy added the subtitle for the book of 1891. The novel is divided into seven Phases, the first called “The Maiden”.

link.label: Tess of the d’Urbervilles study guide

questions.question: Which poet called *The Moonstone* “the first, the longest, and the best of modern English detective novels”?
questions.hint: He wrote an introduction to the novel in 1928.
questions.explanation: Wilkie Collins published *The Moonstone* in 1868. Its detective, Sergeant Cuff, was partly modelled on Inspector Jonathan Whicher.

questions.question: Which character in *The Woman in White* keeps white mice, a cockatoo and canaries?
questions.hint: He is an Italian count of great size.
questions.explanation: Fosco is the friend and adviser of Sir Percival Glyde and the most dangerous person in the book. Marian Halcombe’s diary describes him at length.

questions.question: In which publication did Sherlock Holmes first appear, in 1887?
questions.hint: The story was *A Study in Scarlet*.
questions.explanation: *A Study in Scarlet* appeared in *Beeton’s Christmas Annual* in November 1887. Holmes became famous after the short stories began in *The Strand Magazine* in 1891.

questions.question: Who is always “the woman” to Sherlock Holmes?
questions.hint: She outwits him in “A Scandal in Bohemia”.
questions.explanation: Watson says Holmes never spoke of her under any other title. Irene Adler keeps the photograph the King of Bohemia wanted recovered.

questions.question: At the start of *The Sign of Four*, what is Holmes injecting himself with?
questions.hint: Watson asks which it is today.
questions.explanation: Holmes says he takes the drug when he has no work for his mind. Mary Morstan then arrives with her case.

questions.question: On which moor is *The Hound of the Baskervilles* set?
questions.hint: An escaped convict from Princetown is hiding there.
questions.explanation: The novel was serialised in *The Strand Magazine* in 1901–02. It is set before the events of “The Final Problem”, in which Holmes seemed to have died.

questions.question: On a boat trip on 4 July 1862, Charles Dodgson first told the Alice story to three sisters. What was their surname?
questions.hint: Their father was Dean of Christ Church, Oxford.
questions.explanation: Dodgson rowed Lorina, Alice and Edith Liddell up the Thames to Godstow. Alice asked him to write the story down, and he gave her the manuscript, *Alice’s Adventures under Ground*.

questions.question: Who drew the illustrations for the first edition of *Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland* (1865)?
questions.hint: He was the chief cartoonist of *Punch*.
questions.explanation: Tenniel was unhappy with the printing of the first edition, and Carroll withdrew it. The book was reprinted for the general public later in 1865, dated 1866.

questions.question: What is the name of the Pooters’ house in *The Diary of a Nobody*?
questions.hint: It is in Brickfield Terrace, Holloway.
questions.explanation: Charles Pooter is a City clerk. The book began as a series in *Punch* in 1888–89 and appeared as a book in 1892.

questions.question: What is the name of the dog in *Three Men in a Boat*?
questions.hint: He is a fox terrier.
questions.explanation: Jerome K. Jerome’s book of 1889 follows three friends rowing up the Thames from Kingston to Oxford, with the dog.

questions.question: Where does the first Martian cylinder land in *The War of the Worlds*?
questions.hint: Wells was living in Woking when he wrote the book.
questions.explanation: The cylinder lands on Horsell Common, a short walk from Wells’s house. The Martians later advance on London.

questions.question: What finally kills the Martians in *The War of the Worlds*?
questions.hint: Human beings have built up resistance to it over thousands of years.
questions.explanation: The narrator finds the Martians dead in their machines, killed by bacteria against which they had no defence.

questions.question: In M. R. James’s story “Oh, Whistle, and I’ll Come to You, My Lad”, what does Professor Parkins find in a ruined Templar preceptory?
questions.hint: It carries a Latin inscription.
questions.explanation: Parkins blows the whistle, and something answers. The story was published in *Ghost Stories of an Antiquary* in 1904.

link.label: M. R. James: Collected Ghost Stories

questions.question: In Sheridan Le Fanu’s *Carmilla*, the names Millarca and Mircalla are what?
questions.hint: All three names belong to the same person.
questions.explanation: *Carmilla* appeared as a serial in *The Dark Blue* in 1871–72, more than twenty years before *Dracula*. Her earlier identity is Countess Mircalla Karnstein.

questions.question: What is the name of the house where the governess looks after Miles and Flora in *The Turn of the Screw*?
questions.hint: It is in Essex.
questions.explanation: The children’s uncle hires the governess on condition that she never troubles him about them. Henry James published the story in 1898.

questions.question: Charlotte Perkins Gilman wrote “The Yellow Wall-Paper” after undergoing which physician’s “rest cure”?
questions.hint: He is named in the story.
questions.explanation: The narrator’s husband threatens to send her to “Weir Mitchell in the fall”. Gilman later wrote that she had sent Mitchell a copy of the story.

questions.question: Who commissioned the first commercially printed Christmas card, in 1843?
questions.hint: He later became the first director of what is now the V&A.
questions.explanation: Henry Cole asked the artist John Callcott Horsley to design the card. About a thousand copies were printed and sold for a shilling each.

questions.question: Which London confectioner is credited with inventing the Christmas cracker?
questions.hint: He began by wrapping sugared almonds in paper with a motto.
questions.explanation: Tom Smith sold sweets wrapped in twists of paper from the 1840s and later added the snap, a strip that cracks when the cracker is pulled. The paper hats came later still.

questions.question: Under what title was *Moby-Dick* first published in London in October 1851?
questions.hint: The American edition followed a month later.
questions.explanation: Richard Bentley published *The Whale* in three volumes in London. The London edition left out the Epilogue, so some British reviewers wondered how the narrator had survived.

questions.question: What does Captain Ahab nail to the mainmast as a reward for the first man to sight Moby Dick?
questions.hint: The coin comes from Ecuador.
questions.explanation: Ahab nails the doubloon to the mast in Chapter 36, “The Quarter-Deck”. In Chapter 99 several of the crew look at the coin and each reads it differently.

questions.question: What is the name of Hester Prynne’s daughter in *The Scarlet Letter*?
questions.hint: Her name comes from a parable about something of great price.
questions.explanation: Hester named her Pearl, “as being of great price”, after the parable in Matthew’s Gospel. The father, the minister Arthur Dimmesdale, is not named until late in the book.

questions.question: *The Scarlet Letter* begins with an introduction about Hawthorne’s years in which job?
options: Surveyor at the Salem Custom House
Minister of a church in Concord
questions.hint: He lost the post after a change of government.
questions.explanation: In “The Custom-House”, Hawthorne claims to have found the scarlet letter and an old manuscript about Hester Prynne in the building’s attic.

questions.question: Who travels down the Mississippi on a raft with Huck Finn?
questions.hint: He has run away because he is about to be sold.
questions.explanation: Jim escapes from Miss Watson when he hears she plans to sell him down the river. Huck has faked his own death to get away from his father.

questions.question: Which writer said that “all modern American literature comes from one book by Mark Twain called Huckleberry Finn”?
questions.hint: The remark appears in a book about a hunting trip in Africa.
questions.explanation: Hemingway wrote it in *Green Hills of Africa* (1935). He added that readers should stop at the point where Jim is stolen from the boys.

questions.question: Which chore does Tom Sawyer trick other boys into doing for him?
questions.hint: Aunt Polly sets it as a punishment.
questions.explanation: Tom pretends the work is a privilege, and the other boys pay him with apples, marbles and a dead rat for a turn with the brush.

questions.question: In which summer is *The Great Gatsby* set?
questions.hint: Nick Carraway turns thirty during the novel.
questions.explanation: Nick rents a house in West Egg in the spring of 1922. Fitzgerald published the novel in April 1925.

questions.question: Which title, taken from a character in Petronius’s *Satyricon*, did Fitzgerald consider for *The Great Gatsby*?
questions.hint: The character is a rich former slave who gives lavish feasts.
questions.explanation: Fitzgerald considered several titles, including *Trimalchio in West Egg*, *Under the Red, White, and Blue* and *Among Ash-Heaps and Millionaires*. An early draft has been published as *Trimalchio*.

questions.question: Who first taught Frederick Douglass the alphabet?
options: Sophia Auld, the wife of his enslaver
questions.hint: Her husband stopped the lessons.
questions.explanation: Hugh Auld told his wife that learning would make Douglass unfit to be a slave. Douglass writes that this showed him the “pathway from slavery to freedom”, and he went on learning from boys in the street.

link.label: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

questions.question: Why did Douglass leave out the details of his escape from his *Narrative* of 1845?
options: To protect the people and routes that helped him
Because he had not yet escaped
questions.hint: He described the escape only after slavery had ended.
questions.explanation: Douglass escaped in 1838 dressed as a sailor and carrying borrowed papers. He gave the details in *Life and Times of Frederick Douglass* (1881).

link.label: Narrative of the Life of Frederick Douglass

questions.question: In *Uncle Tom’s Cabin*, how does Eliza escape across the Ohio River with her child?
options: By jumping from one ice floe to the next
questions.hint: The river is breaking up in early spring.
questions.explanation: Eliza runs when she learns her son Harry is to be sold. Harriet Beecher Stowe’s novel was serialised in 1851–52 and published as a book in 1852.

questions.question: Where does Buck live before he is stolen and sold in *The Call of the Wild*?
options: On Judge Miller’s estate in the Santa Clara Valley
In a lumber camp in Oregon
questions.hint: It is in California.
questions.explanation: Buck is stolen by a gardener’s helper who owes gambling debts and is shipped north to be used as a sled dog in the Klondike gold rush of 1897.

questions.question: Stephen Crane published *The Red Badge of Courage*, a novel of the American Civil War, in 1895. When was he born?
questions.hint: He had never seen a battle when he wrote it.
questions.explanation: Crane was born six years after the war ended. He drew on veterans’ accounts, including the series *Battles and Leaders of the Civil War*.

questions.question: Where does Edna Pontellier spend the summer at the start of *The Awakening*?
questions.hint: It is an island resort on the Gulf of Mexico.
questions.explanation: Kate Chopin’s novel of 1899 begins among Creole families on holiday at Grand Isle in Louisiana. Edna learns to swim there.

questions.question: In which fictional New England town is *Ethan Frome* set?
questions.hint: The name suggests a bare winter landscape.
questions.explanation: The unnamed narrator is stuck in Starkfield, Massachusetts, for a winter and pieces together Ethan’s story. Edith Wharton published the novel in 1911.

questions.question: According to the legend in Washington Irving’s story, who was the Headless Horseman in life?
options: A Hessian trooper whose head was carried away by a cannonball
questions.hint: He fought in the American Revolutionary War.
questions.explanation: The story says the trooper rides out each night in search of his head. Ichabod Crane, the schoolmaster, disappears after meeting him.

questions.question: Which detective did Edgar Allan Poe introduce in “The Murders in the Rue Morgue” (1841)?
questions.hint: He lives in Paris.
questions.explanation: Dupin appears in three of Poe’s stories. His unnamed friend narrates them, a pattern Conan Doyle later used for Holmes and Watson.

questions.question: How does Hank Morgan escape being burned at the stake in *A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court*?
options: He claims to cause a solar eclipse
questions.hint: He remembers the date of one from his own century.
questions.explanation: Hank knows an eclipse is due and announces that he will blot out the sun. Mark Twain published the novel in 1889.

link.label: A Connecticut Yankee in King Arthur’s Court

questions.question: What evidence does David Wilson use to solve the murder in *Pudd’nhead Wilson*?
questions.hint: He has collected them from the townspeople for years as a hobby.
questions.explanation: Wilson’s collection proves that two babies were exchanged in their cradles. Mark Twain published the novel in 1894, when fingerprinting was still a new method of identification.

questions.question: In *Anne of Green Gables*, what had Matthew and Marilla Cuthbert asked the orphanage to send?
options: A boy, to help on the farm
questions.hint: The message was passed on wrongly.
questions.explanation: Matthew drives to the station and finds Anne waiting. L. M. Montgomery’s novel of 1908 is set on Prince Edward Island.

questions.question: What news makes Valancy Stirling change her life in L. M. Montgomery’s *The Blue Castle*?
options: A doctor’s letter saying she has a year to live
questions.hint: The letter later turns out to have been meant for someone else.
questions.explanation: Valancy is twenty-nine and has always done what her family wanted. After the letter she leaves home and marries Barney Snaith.

questions.question: In the first sentence of *Mrs Dalloway*, what does Clarissa say she will buy herself?
questions.hint: She is preparing for a party that evening.
questions.explanation: The novel follows one day in June 1923. Clarissa’s party, which ends the book, is the event the day leads to.

questions.question: What was Virginia Woolf’s working title for *Mrs Dalloway*?
questions.hint: Michael Cunningham later used it for a novel.
questions.explanation: Big Ben strikes the hours through the book. Cunningham’s *The Hours* (1998) follows three women connected to *Mrs Dalloway*.

questions.question: *A Room of One’s Own* grew out of lectures Woolf gave in 1928 at which two Cambridge colleges?
questions.hint: Both were colleges for women.
questions.explanation: Woolf spoke on women and fiction in October 1928 and expanded the talks into the book published in 1929.

questions.question: How much money a year does Woolf say a woman needs in order to write fiction?
questions.hint: She also needs a room with a lock on the door.
questions.explanation: Woolf’s narrator inherits five hundred a year from an aunt, which she says freed her from writing for money and from resentment.

questions.question: In *A Room of One’s Own*, whose imagined life does Woolf use to show what would have happened to a woman of genius in the sixteenth century?
questions.hint: Woolf invents her.
questions.explanation: Woolf imagines Judith Shakespeare running away to London to act, being refused, and dying by her own hand. Shakespeare in fact had a sister called Joan.

questions.question: In *Heart of Darkness*, what does Marlow tell Kurtz’s Intended were his last words?
questions.hint: It is a lie.
questions.explanation: Kurtz’s last words were “The horror! The horror!” Marlow, who says he hates lies, cannot bring himself to tell her.

questions.question: Which Nigerian novelist argued in a 1975 lecture that *Heart of Darkness* denies Africans their humanity?
questions.hint: He wrote *Things Fall Apart*.
questions.explanation: Achebe gave the lecture “An Image of Africa” at the University of Massachusetts in 1975. It is one of the most cited essays in the criticism of Conrad.

questions.question: What is Gregor Samsa’s job before his transformation?
questions.hint: He worries about missing his train.
questions.explanation: Gregor supports his parents and sister and hates his work. Kafka himself worked for an accident insurance institute in Prague.

questions.question: In 1915 Kafka wrote to his publisher with an instruction about the cover of *The Metamorphosis*. What was it?
options: The insect itself must not be drawn
It must name him as a lawyer
questions.hint: The first edition shows a man covering his face.
questions.explanation: Kafka asked that the insect not be shown, “not even from a distance”. Ottomar Starke’s cover shows a man in a doorway with his hands over his face.

questions.question: Which poet, then a director at Faber and Faber, turned down *Animal Farm* in 1944?
questions.hint: He wrote that the pigs were “far more intelligent than the other animals”.
questions.explanation: Eliot’s letter argued that what was needed was “not more communism but more public-spirited pigs”. Secker and Warburg published the book in August 1945.

questions.question: How does the last version of the commandments on the barn wall read in *Animal Farm*?
options: All animals are equal but some animals are more equal than others
Four legs good, two legs better
No animal shall sleep in a bed with sheets
Whatever goes upon two legs is a friend
questions.hint: Benjamin reads it out to Clover.
questions.explanation: By the end, the seven commandments have been replaced by this single sentence. The pigs then start to walk on their hind legs.

questions.question: What is the subtitle of G. K. Chesterton’s *The Man Who Was Thursday*?
questions.hint: The ending suggests the whole story may have been a dream.
questions.explanation: Gabriel Syme, a poet turned police detective, joins a council of seven anarchists named after the days of the week. Chesterton published the novel in 1908.

questions.question: Where did T. E. Lawrence lose most of the first draft of *Seven Pillars of Wisdom* in 1919?
questions.hint: He was changing trains.
questions.explanation: Lawrence rewrote the book from memory. A private subscribers’ edition appeared in 1926, and the general edition after his death in 1935.

questions.question: Which poem by Yeats ends “And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?”
questions.hint: It was collected in *Michael Robartes and the Dancer* (1921).
questions.explanation: Yeats wrote the poem in January 1919. The same collection contains “Easter, 1916”.

questions.question: Why has the children’s father gone away in *The Railway Children*?
options: He has been wrongly imprisoned as a spy
He is fighting in a war
He has gone to work abroad
questions.hint: Bobbie finds out from an old newspaper.
questions.explanation: E. Nesbit’s novel was serialised in 1905 and published as a book in 1906. The old gentleman the children wave to on the train helps prove their father innocent.

questions.question: Which chapter title of *The Wind in the Willows* did Pink Floyd use for their first album?
options: The Piper at the Gates of Dawn
questions.hint: In the chapter Rat and Mole meet the god Pan.
questions.explanation: Rat and Mole search the river at night for Otter’s missing son and find him asleep at the feet of Pan. Pink Floyd’s album came out in 1967.

questions.question: On which river are the two travellers canoeing in Algernon Blackwood’s story “The Willows”?
questions.hint: They have come down from Vienna towards Budapest.
questions.explanation: The two men camp on a sandy island among willows as the river floods. Blackwood had made the canoe journey himself.

questions.question: What does Carnacki, William Hope Hodgson’s ghost-finder, use to protect himself?
questions.hint: It is made of vacuum tubes.
questions.explanation: Carnacki combines the electric pentacle with older defences taken from a fictional manuscript he calls the Sigsand. The stories were collected in 1913.

questions.question: For a German production in 1880 Ibsen reluctantly wrote a different ending to *A Doll’s House*. What happens in it?
options: Nora sees her sleeping children and stays
questions.hint: The actress playing Nora had refused to perform the original.
questions.explanation: Ibsen called the alternative ending a “barbaric outrage” and wrote it only so that no one else would. In the original Nora leaves, and the door slams.

questions.question: Where was Jack Worthing found as a baby in *The Importance of Being Earnest*?
options: In a handbag at Victoria Station
On the steps of a church
In a basket on the river
questions.hint: It was the Brighton line.
questions.explanation: Lady Bracknell is appalled. At the end Miss Prism admits she left the baby there and put her three-volume novel in the pram.

questions.question: The saying “We all came out from under Gogol’s Overcoat” is often credited to which novelist, though there is no record of him saying it?
questions.hint: The remark first appears in a French critic’s book about the Russian novel.
questions.explanation: The phrase is found in the writing of Eugène-Melchior de Vogüé, who reported it as something said by a Russian writer. Its attribution to Dostoevsky is usually treated as doubtful.

questions.question: Which work opens “I am a sick man… I am a spiteful man”?
questions.hint: Its narrator is a retired civil servant in St Petersburg.
questions.explanation: Dostoevsky published *Notes from Underground* in 1864. Its first part is a monologue and its second a story from the narrator’s youth.

questions.question: Which of the Karamazov brothers tells the story of the Grand Inquisitor?
questions.hint: He tells it to his younger brother in a tavern.
questions.explanation: Ivan calls the story a poem he has not written down. In it Christ returns to Seville in the time of the Inquisition and is arrested.

questions.question: *The Brothers Karamazov* was the last novel Dostoevsky completed. When did he die?
questions.hint: The novel had finished its serial run only a few months before.
questions.explanation: The novel appeared in *The Russian Messenger* in 1879–80. Dostoevsky died in St Petersburg in February 1881.

questions.question: Over how many nights does Dostoevsky’s *White Nights* take place?
questions.hint: The last section is called “Morning”.
questions.explanation: The narrator, a lonely dreamer, meets Nastenka by the canal and they talk on four successive nights in the St Petersburg summer.

questions.question: How does Ivan Ilyich receive the injury that begins his illness?
options: He falls while showing a workman how to hang curtains
He is thrown from a carriage
He is attacked in the street
He slips on ice outside the courts
questions.hint: He is decorating his new flat.
questions.explanation: Ivan Ilyich knocks his side against a window frame. Tolstoy’s story of 1886 opens with his colleagues hearing of his death.

questions.question: Which Scottish poet wrote a poem called “Halloween”, published in 1786 with notes on the customs it describes?
questions.hint: The poem appeared in his first collection, printed at Kilmarnock.
questions.explanation: Burns describes young people in Ayrshire trying to foretell their future husbands and wives with nuts, kale stalks and apples.

questions.question: Which novel of 1764 is usually called the first Gothic novel?
questions.hint: Its author, Horace Walpole, lived at Strawberry Hill.
questions.explanation: Walpole first presented the book as a translation of an old Italian manuscript. The second edition admitted his authorship and called it “A Gothic Story”.

questions.question: Which writer used the pen name “Boz”?
questions.hint: It came from a family nickname for his younger brother.
questions.explanation: *Sketches by Boz*, Dickens’s first book, was published in 1836. *The Pickwick Papers* began appearing in the same year.

questions.question: Where was Guy Fawkes arrested in November 1605?
options: In a cellar beneath the House of Lords
On a boat on the Thames
questions.hint: He was guarding barrels of gunpowder.
questions.explanation: Fawkes was found around midnight on 4–5 November with thirty-six barrels of gunpowder. Parliament ordered an annual thanksgiving for the King’s escape in 1606.
